fetched_contents.text: Digital learning designs in physiotherapy education: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background Digital learning designs have the potential to support teaching and learning within higher education. However, the research on digital learning designs within physiotherapy education is limited. This study aims to identify and investigate the effectiveness of digital learning designs in physiotherapy education. Methods The study was designed as a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and non-randomized trials. A search of eight databases on digital learning designs and technology was conducted. Study selection, methodology and quality assessment were performed independently by three reviewers. The included studies were mapped according to the types of digital interventions and studies. For similar interventions, the learning effects were calculated using meta-analyses. Results Altogether, 22 studies were included in the review (17 randomized controlled trials and five cohort studies). A blended learning design was used in 21 studies, a flipped classroom model in five and a distance learning design in one. Altogether, 10 of the 22 articles were included in meta-analyses, which showed statistically significant effects for flipped classrooms on knowledge acquisition (standardized mean difference [SMD]: 0.41; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.20, 0.62), for interactive websites or applications (apps) on practical skills (SMD: 1.07; 95% CI: 0.71,1.43) and for students self-produced videos on a practical skill in a cervical spine scenario (SMD: 0.49; 95% CI: 0.06, 0.93). Overall, the effects indicated that blended learning designs are equally as or more effective than traditional classroom teaching to achieve learning outcomes. Distance learning showed no significant differences compared to traditional classroom teaching. Conclusions The current findings from physiotherapy education indicate that digital learning designs in the form of blended learning and distance learning were equally or more effective compared to traditional teaching. The meta-analyses revealed significant effects on student learning in favour of the interventions using flipped classrooms, interactive websites/apps and students self-produced videos. However, these results must be confirmed in larger controlled trials. Further, research should investigate how digital learning designs can facilitate students’ learning of practical skills and behaviour, learning retention and approaches to studying as well as references for teaching and learning in digital learning environments. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12909-020-02483-w. UNESCO [1] emphasizes that digital learning can transform teaching practises, improve the quality and enhance the sustainability of higher education. A digital learning design has been described as a didactic plan that integrates digital learning technology to support students’ learning processes and to achieve constructive alignment between learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities and feedback and assessment methods [2]. The designs can fully or partly integrate digital learning tools and resources (e.g., video lectures or video tutorials) and have the potential to move traditional teaching out of the classroom and to facilitate active learning in the classroom [3]. The various designs provide opportunities to improve self-regulating abilities, facilitate active learning and make the learning process more transparent [4]. Digital learning designs encompass various technologies such as virtual reality, podcasts, apps, serious/educational games, 360° video and animations. These technologies can be directly implemented in the learning activities or combined with other planned learning activities. Because no conceptual framework for digital learning designs exists, similar digital learning designs are often mentioned using different terminology. Digital learning designs can be divided into blended learning (e.g., flipped classrooms) and distance learning (e.g., fully e-learning courses). The main difference is that blended learning combines online and face-to-face teaching and often combine both synchronous learning (real-time, in-person or online) and asynchronous learning (flexible time, online), whereas distance learning is used as a synonym for fully online learning. In distance learning, teaching and learning is facilitated by a web-based system to connect learners, resources and teachers; and it can be completely asynchronous (flexible regarding when the student is online) [5]. There is conflicting evidence of the effectiveness of the different digital learning designs used in physiotherapy and other health professions education. A systematic review on the effects of the flipped classroom approach for the education of health profession students did not reveal compelling evidence for the effectiveness of the method for improving academic outcomes compared to traditional teaching [6]. In contrast, a meta-analysis on the effectiveness of flipped classrooms in health professions education concluded that this approach yields a significant improvement in student learning compared with traditional teaching methods [7]. Another systematic review on blended learning in health professions showed that it has the potential to improve clinical competence among health students and to be more effective than or at least as effective as non-blended learning for knowledge acquisition [8]. fetched_contents.text: Blended Learning is Effective for Physiotherapy Education | Digital Learning Digital learning designs have the potential to support teaching and learning within physiotherapy education however the impact on learning and outcomes is not fully understood. A new systematic review has helped to further our understanding. Digital and online learning transforms both the way we learn and the way we are taught. Digital learning can improve the quality, enhance sustainability and enable inclusive education for all and there are a number of different types and approaches used. Over the past decade physiotherapy education has been gradually integrating a digital approach to learning at all levels of professional development but which approach is best specifically for physiotherapy? Learn More About Digital Learning and Physiotherapy Physiotherapy curriculums are characterised by a combination of theory, skills training and learning in practice and until now digital learning has not been fully embraced by our profession and has been criticised for not being grounded from a theoretical learning perspective. This is interesting as for a long time there has been evidence to demonstrate the effectiveness of using digital learning for healthcare education. Prior to the covid-19 pandemic digital learning had been under researched in the physiotherapy profession but there has been a boom in interest since for obvious reasons. A new systematic review has aimed to readress this balance by identifying and investigating the effectiveness of digital learning designs in physiotherapy education. A Breakdown: Commonly Used Digital Learning Designs Digital learning designs use lots of different technologies and there are a number of different methods. The language used is difficult and confusing to understand, so below is a breakdown of the most commonly used digital learning strategies. Blended Learning Blended learning is the thoughtful integration of classroom face-to-face learning experiences with online learning experiences. A lot of students and teachers do this already. It is basically the use of integrating face-to-face / same-time (synchronous) and flexible-time learning (asynchronous) activities together. Simply put the combination of learning the same things at the same time as others and learning the same things as others in your own time. Examples of Blended Learning Models Flipped Classroom Model: In a flipped classroom the traditional face-to-face lecture is done prior to the classroom and the learning in-class is active, collaborative task and problem-solving focussed. After class they follow up and consolidate their knowledge Blended Learning On & Off Campus: An example of blended learning design is where the students, for example, gain access to digital learning resources prior to in-class teaching and/or after classroom teaching, but the teaching is traditionally offered. Another example is that the learning activities in the classroom teaching are given and answered through digital learning technology and software. Hybrid Learning: One student group follows the course on campus and at the same time another group follows the course remotely through digital technology. Hybrid learning can combine synchronous learning with asynchronous learning elements. Distance Learning Distance learning is planned learning that occurs in a different place from teaching and requires special course design and methods of communication by electronic and other technology, as well as formalised organisational and administrative arrangements. Examples of Distance Learning Models E-learning Courses: a structured course delivered electronically with different elements: live or pre-recorded lecture content, video, quizzes, simulations, games, activities, and other interactive elements. E-learning can also be facilitated as virtual classrooms – a type of online learning in which live interaction between instructors and participants take place at the same time. Mobile Learning: Variant of e-learning where teaching takes place via mobile equipment. Remote/at-home Learning: A course designed to be delivered online, not intended to meet in-person, students intended not to work on assignments in the same space, and do not attend lectures or classes virtually with video or audio communication to participate. Massive Open Online Courses (MOOC): A massive open online course is an online course aimed at unlimited participation and open access via the web. MOOC integrates the connectivity of social networking, the facilitation of an acknowledged expert in a field of study, and a collection of freely accessible online resources. fetched_contents.text: Spaced Digital Education for Health Professionals: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Background Spaced digital education applies digital tools to deliver educational content via multiple, repeated learning sessions separated by prespecified time intervals. Spaced digital education appears to promote acquisition and long-term retention of knowledge, skills, and change in clinical behavior. Objective The aim of this review was to assess the effectiveness of spaced digital education in improving pre- and postregistration health care professionals’ knowledge, skills, attitudes, satisfaction, and change in clinical behavior. Methods This review followed Cochrane’s methodology and PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) reporting guidelines. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, CINAHL, CENTRAL, and ProQuest Dissertation and Theses databases from January 1990 to February 2023. We included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster RCTs, and quasi-RCTs comparing spaced digital education with nonspaced education, spaced nondigital education, traditional learning, or no intervention for pre- or postregistration health care professionals. Study selection, data extraction, study quality, and certainty of evidence were assessed by 2 independent reviewers. Meta-analyses were conducted using random effect models. Results We included 23 studies evaluating spaced online education (n=17, 74%) or spaced digital simulation (n=6, 26%) interventions. Most studies assessed 1 or 2 outcomes, including knowledge (n=15, 65%), skills (n=9, 39%), attitudes (n=8, 35%), clinical behavior change (n=8, 35%), and satisfaction (n=7, 30%). Most studies had an unclear or a high risk of bias (n=19, 83%). Spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge (n=9, 39%; standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.51, I2=66%, moderate certainty of evidence). Spaced online education (n=3, 13%) was superior to massed online education (n=2, 9%) and no intervention (n=1, 4%; SMD 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-0.91, I2=5%, moderate certainty of evidence) for postintervention clinical behavior change. fetched_contents.text: The Use of Digital Technologies in Physiotherapy Higher Education: a Mixed-Methods Study ABSTRACT Background: Previous studies demonstrated that digital tools can be effectively integrated into physiotherapy higher education. However, their adoption remains limited. This study aimed to 1) evaluate the perceived knowledge, confidence, and frequency of digital technology use among Italian lecturers and 2) explore lecturers’ experiences with digital technology in higher education. Methods: We performed a convergent mixed-method study using an online survey instrument for Italian physiotherapy lectures. We employed a 5-point Likert to evaluate perceived knowledge, confidence, and frequency of digital technology use, with consensus defined as an agreement of ≥70% on a statement. An optional qualitative section explored lecturers’ experiences with technology, which we analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Results: Between June and September 2023, 118 lecturers (mean age: 45 ± 11; 69% female, n = 81) completed the survey. Participants expressed confidence in utilizing digital tools such as videoconferencing (95%), online repositories (88%), and communication apps (78%). On average, 32% reported using technologies “often” or “always.” In the qualitative section, completed by 77 participants, we generated three themes: 1) “Technology can promote a constructive educational approach”; 2) “Action of technologies on students’ learning process,” with mixed results on their impact; and 3) “Technology is not within everyone’s reach,” due to barriers to its implementation in didactics. Qualitative and quantitative findings confirmed one another, allowing for a deeper understanding of digital technologies among Italian physiotherapy lecturers. Conclusions: Our findings indicate that digital tools are still underutilized among Italian physiotherapy lecturers. Deep-research report for N7: Compare the technology types used in physiotherapy digital learning

In physiotherapy education, the most common digital learning technologies are blended learning, flipped classrooms, online modules, video lectures, interactive apps, simulations, and virtual reality. The systematic review and meta-analysis identifies blended learning as the dominant digital learning design in 21 of the 22 included studies, with flipped classrooms in five studies and distance learning in one study [N2-F1]. The review also notes that digital learning designs encompass a range of technologies such as video lectures, video tutorials, podcasts, apps, serious/educational games, 360° video, animations, virtual reality, and immersive simulations [N2-F1]. A separate search result emphasizes that flipped classroom models can integrate virtual patients and active learning tools, while BodyInteract’s flipped classroom with virtual patients is described as an example of how immersive technologies can be used in medical education [N1-R2][N1-R4]. Additional evidence suggests that physiotherapy curricula increasingly use online resources, learning management systems, online repositories, synchronous/asynchronous e-learning technologies, social media, communication apps, and forums [N5-F4].

The evidence supports a clear distinction between formats that are broadly used and those that are more specialized. Video lectures and online modules appear to be among the most common and accessible formats because they are easy to deliver, widely used in blended learning, and often used as pre-class content in flipped classrooms [N2-F1][N5-F4]. Flipped classroom models are particularly notable for their hybrid structure, in which students engage with lecture material before class and then participate in active, collaborative tasks in class [N2-F1][N2-F2]. Interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos are also cited as digital tools that can support practical skills, though the review emphasizes that these effects were significant for practical skills rather than theoretical knowledge [N2-F1]. Virtual reality and immersive technologies are mentioned as part of the broader digital learning toolkit, but they are not yet the most common in the evidence base [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4].

Each format has different strengths and limitations for knowledge acquisition. Video lectures and online modules are useful for delivering content efficiently, but they are often passive and may not promote active recall or spaced learning [N2-F1]. Flipped classrooms are more active and structured to encourage post-class engagement and collaborative problem-solving, which can support knowledge consolidation [N2-F1][N2-F2]. Interactive apps and self-produced videos can make learning more engaging and personalized, but the review notes that their effects were stronger for practical skills than for theoretical knowledge [N2-F1]. Simulations and virtual reality are promising for practical training, but the evidence here is thinner and more specialized [N1-R3][N1-R4]. Distance learning is also included, but the review states that it showed no significant difference compared to traditional classroom teaching, suggesting it may be less effective than blended learning for many outcomes [N2-F1].

For theoretical vs practical content, the evidence suggests that some technologies are better suited to one domain than the other. Blended learning and flipped classrooms appear to support both theoretical and practical learning, but the review emphasizes that flipped classrooms showed a significant effect on knowledge acquisition overall, while interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos showed stronger effects on practical skills [N2-F1]. The more specialized immersive and simulation-based tools are especially relevant for practical training, but the provided evidence does not support them as the best tools for purely theoretical knowledge acquisition [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4]. In contrast, video lectures and online modules are more commonly used for theoretical delivery because they are scalable and can be used as pre-class content in blended learning, but they are less likely to promote active recall or long-term retention on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4].

Overall, the evidence points to a pattern: blended learning and flipped classroom designs are the most common and most effective overall, video lectures and online modules are widely used but more passive, and interactive apps, simulations, and virtual reality are promising for practical training but less clearly established as superior for theory [N2-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. The strongest theoretical support is still concentrated in blended learning and flipped classroom formats rather than in the more specialized immersive tools cited in the search results [N2-F1][N2-F2].

Deep-research report for N8: Summarize the evidence on effectiveness for theoretical knowledge acquisition

The evidence base indicates that digital learning designs can be effective for theoretical knowledge acquisition, but the strength of the evidence and the type of technology matter. The systematic review and meta-analysis reports that flipped classrooms showed a statistically significant effect on knowledge acquisition, with a standardized mean difference of 0.41 (95% CI: 0.20, 0.62) [N2-F1]. It also found that blended learning designs were equally as or more effective than traditional classroom teaching overall, and that the meta-analyses included in the review supported flipped classrooms and interactive websites/apps for practical skills, though not specifically as evidence for theoretical knowledge [N2-F1]. A separate systematic review and meta-analysis on spaced digital education found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge, with an SMD of 0.32 (95% CI: 0.13–0.51), and that spaced digital education positively impacted confidence and satisfaction [N4-F3]. This is especially relevant to theoretical knowledge because spaced learning is explicitly associated with long-term retention and retrieval, which are critical for theoretical recall.

The study designs and outcome measures differ across the evidence. The review on digital learning designs included randomized controlled trials and cohort studies, and the outcomes were student satisfaction, student perception of learning, learning outcomes, and final grades [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review used randomized controlled trials, cluster RCTs, and quasi-RCTs, with outcomes including knowledge, skills, attitudes, clinical behavior change, and satisfaction [N4-F3]. The key difference is that the digital learning designs review is broader and includes both theoretical and practical outcomes, while the spaced digital education review is narrower and more focused on knowledge and behavior change [N2-F1][N4-F3]. In the physiotherapy-specific evidence, one study assessed theoretical acquisition and practical skills using MCQs, but the results were not statistically significant, highlighting that the evidence for some formats can be mixed or limited [N6-R1]. Another study on physiotherapy education notes that distance learning can be less effective than blended learning and that the evidence on digital learning designs is still emerging [N2-F1].

The effects do not appear to be uniform across all learners or content depths, but the evidence provided is limited in this respect. The digital learning designs review did not report major differences by learner background, but it did emphasize that the effects varied by intervention type and that the findings must be confirmed in larger controlled trials [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review also did not find strong evidence of differences by learner background, and it reported only moderate certainty for knowledge outcomes and low certainty for surgical skills [N4-F3]. The most relevant theoretical outcome in the physiotherapy evidence is that flipped classrooms had a significant effect on knowledge acquisition, while interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos showed significant effects on practical skills [N2-F1]. This suggests that effectiveness may depend more on the format and whether the content is theory-heavy or practice-oriented than on learner characteristics alone [N2-F1].

For theoretical knowledge acquisition specifically, the strongest evidence in the provided material is for flipped classrooms and for spaced digital education. Flipped classrooms are supported by a meta-analysis showing a significant effect on knowledge acquisition [N2-F1], while spaced online education is supported by a meta-analysis showing superiority over massed online education for knowledge [N4-F3]. The evidence is thinner for other formats, and the review explicitly notes that the findings must be confirmed in larger controlled trials [N2-F1]. Overall, the evidence favors blended and flipped learning structures for theoretical knowledge, with spaced learning as a complementary method that improves retention and recall, while the most direct evidence for practical skills is stronger than for purely theoretical outcomes [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Deep-research report for N9: Summarize the blended education context and implementation factors

Blended learning in physiotherapy education is defined as the thoughtful integration of classroom face-to-face learning experiences with online learning experiences, combining synchronous and asynchronous learning activities [N3-R1][N2-F2]. In practice, this means students may access digital learning resources before class, during class, or after class, while face-to-face teaching remains an important component of the curriculum [N2-F2]. The review on digital learning designs explicitly states that blended learning combines online and face-to-face teaching and often combines both synchronous learning and asynchronous learning [N2-F1]. It also describes blended learning on- and off-campus models, hybrid learning, and blended learning as a general approach where students gain access to digital learning resources prior to or after classroom teaching [N2-F2]. This structure is especially relevant to physiotherapy education because curricula combine theory, skills training, and practice, and blended learning can therefore support both pre-class content delivery and in-class active learning [N2-F2][N6-R2].

Implementation factors that improve effectiveness include careful planning, lecturer confidence, infrastructure, student-centered tools, clear instructions, flexible and accessible resources, effective feedback mechanisms, and integration of authentic virtual environments [N5-F4]. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies in physiotherapy higher education found that lecturers reported confidence in using videoconferencing, online repositories, and communication apps, but that use remained limited due to inadequate infrastructure and lack of digital competencies [N5-F4]. It also identified mixed results on the impact of digital technologies, suggesting that implementation quality is critical [N5-F4]. The systematic review on digital learning designs found that blended learning was equally as or more effective than traditional classroom teaching overall, and that flipped classrooms were among the most effective interventions [N2-F1]. This suggests that blended learning is not inherently effective; its success depends on how it is structured and implemented.

Implementation factors that hinder effectiveness include inadequate infrastructure, limited lecturer confidence, inconsistent use, and lack of digital competencies [N5-F4]. The review also notes that successful adoption requires careful planning, collaborative efforts among educators, student-centered tools, clear instructions, flexible and accessible resources, effective feedback mechanisms, and integration of authentic virtual environments [N5-F4]. The physiotherapy-specific evidence also points to organizational issues such as large class sizes as barriers to adopting digital technologies [N5-R1]. These factors are especially relevant in blended learning because the digital and face-to-face components must be carefully aligned to avoid fragmentation or overload.

Curriculum design and instructor support are central to learning outcomes. The review on digital learning designs emphasizes that digital learning designs can be divided into blended learning and distance learning, and that the main difference is that blended learning combines online and face-to-face teaching [N2-F1]. It also states that digital learning designs can improve self-regulating abilities, facilitate active learning, and make the learning process more transparent [N2-F1]. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies found that lecturers’ technical skills, adaptability, and ongoing professional development are crucial for effective integration [N5-F4]. Instructors’ confidence and ability to use technology influence whether digital resources are used consistently and effectively [N5-F4]. Curriculum design matters because blended learning must map learning outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment methods to digital and face-to-face components [N2-F1]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which blended learning is most effective when curriculum design is coherent, instructor support is strong, and implementation is supported by adequate infrastructure and training [N2-F1][N5-F4].

Deep-research report for N10: Summarize how content type and learning method shape effectiveness

The evidence suggests that theoretical and practical content affect technology effectiveness in different ways. In physiotherapy education, curricula combine theory, skills training, and practice, and the review notes that distance learning can be less effective than blended learning [N2-F1][N6-R2]. The evidence also indicates that interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos showed significant effects on practical skills, while the most direct theoretical evidence comes from flipped classrooms and spaced digital education [N2-F1][N4-F3]. This implies that some technologies are better suited to practical training than to theoretical knowledge acquisition, while blended and flipped designs appear to support both domains more effectively [N2-F1][N2-F2].

Study outcomes do differ by content domain. The digital learning designs review explicitly includes both theoretical acquisition and practical skills outcomes, and the meta-analyses show that flipped classrooms had a significant effect on knowledge acquisition, while interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos had significant effects on practical skills [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review also found that spaced online education improved knowledge and that spaced digital simulation improved surgical skills, showing that the effectiveness of spaced learning can vary by the nature of the content being learned [N4-F3]. The physiotherapy-specific evidence on theoretical and practical content also notes that distance learning has limitations for active skill acquisition, reinforcing the idea that the same technology may be more appropriate for one domain than another [N6-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports a domain-specific pattern: flipped classrooms and spaced learning are especially relevant for theoretical knowledge, while interactive and simulation-based tools are more relevant for practical skills [N2-F1][N4-F3][N6-R3].

The evidence also shows that digital tools can support or interfere with theoretical knowledge acquisition depending on how they are used. Video lectures and online modules are widely used in blended learning and flipped classrooms, but they are often passive and may not promote active recall or spaced repetition on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4]. In contrast, flipped classrooms are structured to encourage post-class engagement and collaborative tasks, which can support knowledge consolidation [N2-F1][N2-F2]. Spaced digital education is explicitly designed to improve long-term retention and recall, and the review found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge [N4-F3]. This suggests that digital tools that incorporate active retrieval and spaced learning can support theoretical knowledge acquisition, whereas tools that merely deliver content passively may not do so as effectively [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that the review on digital learning designs found no significant difference for theoretical acquisition in one study, indicating that effectiveness can vary across studies and may not be uniform [N6-R1].

The evidence provided does not strongly establish systematic differences by learner background in the theoretical context, but it does emphasize that effects vary by intervention type and that the findings must be confirmed in larger controlled trials [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review reported moderate certainty for knowledge outcomes and low certainty for surgical skills, suggesting that study design and outcome measures also shape the interpretation of effectiveness [N4-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that theoretical knowledge acquisition is better supported by blended learning, flipped classrooms, and spaced digital education, while practical skills are better supported by interactive and simulation-based tools [N2-F1][N4-F3][N6-R3]. The same technology may therefore be more or less effective depending on whether the content is theoretical or practical [N2-F1][N4-F3][N6-R3].

# Final synthesis: How different digital learning technologies compare in effectiveness for theoretical knowledge acquisition in blended physiotherapy education

## 1) Overall conclusion: blended learning and flipped classrooms are the strongest overall, but evidence varies by technology and content

The evidence suggests that blended learning and flipped classrooms are the most effective digital learning designs for theoretical knowledge acquisition in physiotherapy education, while video lectures and online modules are widely used but less clearly superior on their own [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The systematic review and meta-analysis found that blended learning designs were equally as or more effective than traditional classroom teaching overall, and that flipped classrooms showed a statistically significant effect on knowledge acquisition (SMD: 0.41) [N2-F1]. In contrast, the same review found that interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos showed significant effects on practical skills, not theoretical knowledge [N2-F1]. A separate meta-analysis on spaced digital education also found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge, with an SMD of 0.32 [N4-F3]. Taken together, the evidence points to a hierarchy: flipped classrooms and spaced learning are especially relevant for theoretical knowledge, while blended learning provides the overall blended-education context in which these tools are most likely to be effective [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

## 2) Which technologies are most common in physiotherapy education?

The most common digital learning technologies in physiotherapy education are blended learning, flipped classrooms, video lectures, online modules, interactive websites/apps, simulations, virtual reality, and immersive technologies [N2-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4]. The review explicitly identifies these as part of the broader digital learning toolkit, with virtual reality, podcasts, apps, serious/educational games, 360° video, animations, and immersive simulations all appearing in the literature [N2-F1]. A separate source highlights that flipped classroom models can integrate virtual patients and active learning tools, while BodyInteract’s flipped classroom with virtual patients is presented as an example of how immersive technologies can be used in medical education [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies in physiotherapy higher education also notes that common tools include learning management systems, online repositories, communication apps, videoconferencing, forums, and audience response systems [N5-F4].

## 3) How each technology format supports or limits knowledge acquisition

### Video lectures and online modules
These are widely used and accessible, but they are often passive and may not promote active recall or spaced learning on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4]. They are useful for delivering content efficiently and as pre-class content in blended learning, but the evidence suggests they are less likely to support deep theoretical retention unless combined with active learning activities [N2-F1][N5-F4].

### Flipped classrooms
Flipped classrooms are particularly strong for theoretical knowledge acquisition. The review reports that flipped classrooms had a statistically significant effect on knowledge acquisition, and the broader literature describes them as a hybrid model in which students engage with lecture material before class and then participate in active, collaborative tasks in class [N2-F1][N2-F2]. This structure supports post-class consolidation and active learning, which is important for theoretical knowledge retention [N2-F2].

### Interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos
These are noted as tools that can support practical skills, but the review’s strongest theoretical evidence is for flipped classrooms rather than for interactive apps or self-produced videos [N2-F1]. The review also reports that these effects were significant for practical skills rather than for theoretical knowledge [N2-F1].

### Simulations and virtual reality
These are promising for practical training, but the evidence provided is thinner and more specialized [N1-R3][N1-R4]. They are less clearly established as superior for theoretical knowledge acquisition in the available sources [N2-F1].

### Distance learning
Distance learning was included in the review but showed no significant difference compared to traditional classroom teaching overall [N2-F1]. This suggests it is not the best standalone model for theoretical knowledge acquisition in physiotherapy education.

### Spaced digital education
Spaced digital education is explicitly designed to improve long-term retention and recall, and the meta-analysis found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge [N4-F3]. This makes it especially relevant for theoretical knowledge acquisition because it supports spaced learning and active retrieval, which are key for recall and retention [N4-F3].

## 4) Which technologies are best suited for theoretical vs practical content?

The evidence clearly supports a domain-specific pattern:

- **Theoretical content**: blended learning, flipped classrooms, and spaced digital education are best suited [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].
- **Practical content**: interactive websites/apps, students’ self-produced videos, and simulation-based tools are better supported [N2-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4].

The review also notes that physiotherapy curricula combine theory, skills training, and practice, which explains why some digital learning designs are used more for one domain than another [N6-R2]. In particular, the evidence suggests that distance learning has limitations for active skill acquisition, reinforcing the idea that the same technology may be more appropriate for one domain than the other [N6-R3]. The spaced digital education review also found that spaced online education improved knowledge and that spaced digital simulation improved surgical skills, showing that content type affects effectiveness [N4-F3].

## 5) How blended learning structures combine digital and face-to-face components

Blended learning in physiotherapy education is defined as the thoughtful integration of classroom face-to-face learning experiences with online learning experiences, combining synchronous and asynchronous learning activities [N3-R1][N2-F2]. The review describes blended learning as a design that can include online and face-to-face teaching and often combines both synchronous learning and asynchronous learning [N2-F1]. In practice, this means students may access digital learning resources before class, during class, or after class, while face-to-face teaching remains an important component [N2-F2]. The review also describes blended learning on- and off-campus models, hybrid learning, and blended learning as a general approach where students gain access to digital learning resources prior to or after classroom teaching [N2-F2].

This structure is especially relevant for theoretical knowledge acquisition because blended learning can support both content delivery and active consolidation. The review notes that digital learning designs can improve self-regulating abilities, facilitate active learning, and make the learning process more transparent [N2-F1]. In other words, blended learning is not just a combination of formats; it is a pedagogical structure that can align theory, active learning, and assessment more effectively than a single mode alone [N2-F1].

## 6) Implementation factors that improve or hinder effectiveness

Implementation quality is a major determinant of effectiveness. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies in physiotherapy higher education found that lecturers reported confidence in using videoconferencing, online repositories, and communication apps, but that use remained limited due to inadequate infrastructure and lack of digital competencies [N5-F4]. It also identified mixed results on the impact of digital technologies, suggesting that implementation quality matters [N5-F4]. The review on digital learning designs also emphasizes that successful adoption requires careful planning, collaborative efforts among educators, student-centered tools, clear instructions, flexible and accessible resources, effective feedback mechanisms, and integration of authentic virtual environments [N5-F4].

On the other hand, implementation factors that hinder effectiveness include inadequate infrastructure, limited lecturer confidence, inconsistent use, and lack of digital competencies [N5-F4]. The review also notes organizational issues such as large class sizes as barriers to adopting digital technologies [N5-R1]. These factors are especially relevant in blended learning because the digital and face-to-face components must be carefully aligned to avoid fragmentation or overload.

## 7) How curriculum design and instructor support affect learning outcomes

Curriculum design and instructor support are central to effectiveness. The review on digital learning designs emphasizes that digital learning designs must map learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and feedback and assessment methods [N2-F1]. It also states that digital learning designs can improve self-regulating abilities, facilitate active learning, and make the learning process more transparent [N2-F1]. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies found that lecturers’ technical skills, adaptability, and ongoing professional development are crucial for effective integration [N5-F4]. Instructors’ confidence and ability to use technology influence whether digital resources are used consistently and effectively [N5-F4].

Curriculum design matters because blended learning must be coherent across digital and face-to-face components. The review’s discussion of blended learning and distance learning also highlights that the main difference between them is that blended learning combines online and face-to-face teaching [N2-F1]. This means that theoretical knowledge acquisition is most likely to be supported when the curriculum is carefully aligned to both modes of learning, rather than when digital resources are simply added without restructuring the learning experience [N2-F1][N5-F4].

## 8) Study design and outcome measures differ across studies

The evidence base is mixed in terms of study design and outcome measures. The digital learning designs review included randomized controlled trials and cohort studies, with outcomes including student satisfaction, student perception of learning, learning outcomes, and final grades [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review used randomized controlled trials, cluster RCTs, and quasi-RCTs, with outcomes including knowledge, skills, attitudes, clinical behavior change, and satisfaction [N4-F3]. The key difference is that the digital learning designs review is broader and includes both theoretical and practical outcomes, while the spaced digital education review is narrower and more focused on knowledge and behavior change [N2-F1][N4-F3].

This matters because the interpretation of effectiveness depends on the outcome measure. The physiotherapy-specific evidence on theoretical and practical content also notes that one study assessed theoretical acquisition and practical skills using MCQs, but the results were not statistically significant [N6-R1]. This shows that the evidence is not always uniform, and that effects may vary by study design and outcome measure [N2-F1][N4-F3].

## 9) Whether effects vary by learner background or content depth

The evidence provided is limited on learner background, but it does suggest that effects vary by intervention type. The digital learning designs review notes that the findings must be confirmed in larger controlled trials and that effects vary by intervention type [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review also did not find strong evidence of differences by learner background, and it reported moderate certainty for knowledge outcomes and low certainty for surgical skills [N4-F3]. The most relevant theoretical outcome in the physiotherapy evidence is that flipped classrooms had a significant effect on knowledge acquisition, while interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos showed significant effects on practical skills [N2-F1].

In other words, the evidence does not strongly support broad differences by learner background, but it does indicate that effectiveness is not uniform across all learners or all technologies. The strongest theoretical evidence is still concentrated in flipped classrooms and spaced digital education rather than in the more specialized immersive or simulation-based tools cited in the search results [N2-F1][N4-F3].

## 10) How digital tools support or interfere with theoretical knowledge acquisition

Digital tools can support theoretical knowledge acquisition when they incorporate active retrieval and spaced learning. Spaced digital education is explicitly designed to improve long-term retention and recall, and the meta-analysis found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that digital learning should be structured around retrieval practice and spacing rather than passive content delivery.

In contrast, some digital tools can interfere with theoretical knowledge acquisition if they are used passively. Video lectures and online modules are widely used, but they are often passive and may not promote active recall or spaced repetition on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that interactive apps and self-produced videos are more relevant for practical skills than for theoretical knowledge acquisition [N2-F1]. This implies that digital tools should be matched to the learning goal: passive delivery for exposure, but active retrieval and spaced review for retention [N4-F3][N2-F1].

## 11) Practical implication for blended physiotherapy education

For blended physiotherapy education, the most defensible recommendation is to use flipped classrooms and spaced digital education as the core theoretical-learning formats, supported by blended learning structures that combine digital and face-to-face components [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. Video lectures and online modules are useful for content delivery but should be used in ways that promote active learning and spaced review [N2-F1][N5-F4]. Interactive and simulation-based tools are best used for practical skills rather than as the primary vehicle for theoretical knowledge acquisition [N2-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. Blended learning is most effective when curriculum design is coherent, instructor support is strong, and implementation is supported by adequate infrastructure and training [N2-F1][N5-F4].

## 12) Final comparative ranking

Based on the evidence provided, here is a rough comparative ranking for theoretical knowledge acquisition in blended physiotherapy education:

1. **Flipped classrooms** – strongest direct evidence for knowledge acquisition [N2-F1].
2. **Spaced digital education** – especially effective for long-term retention and recall [N4-F3].
3. **Blended learning** – overall most effective digital learning design, especially when flipped classroom principles are embedded [N2-F1][N2-F2].
4. **Video lectures and online modules** – widely used but less clearly superior for theory on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4].
5. **Interactive websites/apps and self-produced videos** – stronger evidence for practical skills than for theoretical knowledge [N2-F1].
6. **Simulations and virtual reality** – promising for practical training, less clearly established for theory [N1-R3][N1-R4].
7. **Distance learning** – no significant difference compared to traditional teaching overall [N2-F1].

## 13) Bottom line

The evidence supports a clear but nuanced conclusion: blended learning and flipped classrooms are the most effective digital learning designs for theoretical knowledge acquisition in physiotherapy education, while spaced learning is especially useful for retention and recall [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. Video lectures and online modules are common but less clearly superior on their own; interactive and simulation-based tools are better suited to practical skills [N2-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. Implementation quality, curriculum design, and instructor support are critical, and the best outcomes occur when digital tools are used to support active learning and spaced retrieval rather than passive exposure [N2-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

## 1) Overall conclusion: blended learning and flipped classrooms are the strongest overall, but evidence varies by technology and content

A separate meta-analysis on spaced digital education also found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge, with an SMD of 0.32 [N4-F3]. Taken together, the evidence points to a hierarchy: flipped classrooms and spaced learning are especially relevant for theoretical knowledge, while blended learning provides the overall blended-education context in which these tools are most likely to be effective [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

## 2) Which technologies are most common in physiotherapy education?

The most common digital learning technologies in physiotherapy education are blended learning, flipped classrooms, video lectures, online modules, interactive websites/apps, simulations, virtual reality, and immersive technologies [N2-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4]. The review explicitly identifies these as part of the broader digital learning toolkit, with virtual reality, podcasts, apps, serious/educational games, 360° video, animations, and immersive simulations all appearing in the literature [N2-F1]. A separate source highlights that flipped classroom models can integrate virtual patients and active learning tools, while BodyInteract’s flipped classroom with virtual patients is presented as an example of how immersive technologies can be used in medical education [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies in physiotherapy higher education also notes that common tools include learning management systems, online repositories, communication apps, videoconferencing, forums, and audience response systems [N5-F4].

## 3) How each technology format supports or limits knowledge acquisition

### Video lectures and online modules
These are widely used and accessible, but they are often passive and may not promote active recall or spaced learning on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4]. They are useful for delivering content efficiently and as pre-class content in blended learning, but the evidence suggests they are less likely to support deep theoretical retention unless combined with active learning activities [N2-F1][N5-F4].

### Flipped classrooms
Flipped classrooms are particularly strong for theoretical knowledge acquisition. The review reports that flipped classrooms had a statistically significant effect on knowledge acquisition, and the broader literature describes them as a hybrid model in which students engage with lecture material before class and then participate in active, collaborative tasks in class [N2-F1][N2-F2]. This structure supports post-class consolidation and active learning, which is important for theoretical knowledge retention [N2-F2].

### Interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos
These are noted as tools that can support practical skills, but the review’s strongest theoretical evidence is for flipped classrooms rather than for interactive apps or self-produced videos [N2-F1]. The review also reports that these effects were significant for practical skills rather than for theoretical knowledge [N2-F1].

### Simulations and virtual reality
These are promising for practical training, but the evidence provided is thinner and more specialized [N1-R3][N1-R4]. They are less clearly established as superior for theoretical knowledge acquisition in the available sources [N2-F1].

### Distance learning
Distance learning was included in the review but showed no significant difference compared to traditional classroom teaching overall [N2-F1]. This suggests it is not the best standalone model for theoretical knowledge acquisition in physiotherapy education.

### Spaced digital education
Spaced digital education is explicitly designed to improve long-term retention and recall, and the meta-analysis found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge [N4-F3]. This makes it especially relevant for theoretical knowledge acquisition because it supports spaced learning and active retrieval, which are key for recall and retention [N4-F3].

## 4) Which technologies are best suited for theoretical vs practical content?

The evidence clearly supports a domain-specific pattern:

- **Theoretical content**: blended learning, flipped classrooms, and spaced digital education are best suited [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].
- **Practical content**: interactive websites/apps, students’ self-produced videos, and simulation-based tools are better supported [N2-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4].

The review also notes that physiotherapy curricula combine theory, skills training, and practice, which explains why some digital learning designs are used more for one domain than another [N6-R2]. In particular, the evidence suggests that distance learning has limitations for active skill acquisition, reinforcing the idea that the same technology may be more appropriate for one domain than the other [N6-R3]. The spaced digital education review also found that spaced online education improved knowledge and that spaced digital simulation improved surgical skills, showing that content type affects effectiveness [N4-F3].

## 5) How blended learning structures combine digital and face-to-face components

Blended learning in physiotherapy education is defined as the thoughtful integration of classroom face-to-face learning experiences with online learning experiences, combining synchronous and asynchronous learning activities [N3-R1][N2-F2]. The review describes blended learning as a design that can include online and face-to-face teaching and often combines both synchronous learning and asynchronous learning [N2-F1]. In practice, this means students may access digital learning resources before class, during class, or after class, while face-to-face teaching remains an important component [N2-F2]. The review also describes blended learning on- and off-campus models, hybrid learning, and blended learning as a general approach where students gain access to digital learning resources prior to or after classroom teaching [N2-F2].

This structure is especially relevant for theoretical knowledge acquisition because blended learning can support both content delivery and active consolidation. The review notes that digital learning designs can improve self-regulating abilities, facilitate active learning, and make the learning process more transparent [N2-F1]. In other words, blended learning is not just a combination of formats; it is a pedagogical structure that can align theory, active learning, and assessment more effectively than a single mode alone [N2-F1].

## 6) Implementation factors that improve or hinder effectiveness

Implementation quality is a major determinant of effectiveness. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies in physiotherapy higher education found that lecturers reported confidence in using videoconferencing, online repositories, and communication apps, but that use remained limited due to inadequate infrastructure and lack of digital competencies [N5-F4]. It also identified mixed results on the impact of digital technologies, suggesting that implementation quality matters [N5-F4]. These factors are especially relevant in blended learning because the digital and face-to-face components must be carefully aligned to avoid fragmentation or overload.

## 7) How curriculum design and instructor support affect learning outcomes

Curriculum design and instructor support are central to effectiveness. The review on digital learning designs emphasizes that digital learning designs must map learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and feedback and assessment methods [N2-F1]. It also states that digital learning designs can improve self-regulating abilities, facilitate active learning, and make the learning process more transparent [N2-F1]. The mixed-methods study on digital technologies found that lecturers’ technical skills, adaptability, and ongoing professional development are crucial for effective integration [N5-F4]. ## 8) Study design and outcome measures differ across studies

The evidence base is mixed in terms of study design and outcome measures. The digital learning designs review included randomized controlled trials and cohort studies, with outcomes including student satisfaction, student perception of learning, learning outcomes, and final grades [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review used randomized controlled trials, cluster RCTs, and quasi-RCTs, with outcomes including knowledge, skills, attitudes, clinical behavior change, and satisfaction [N4-F3]. This matters because the interpretation of effectiveness depends on the outcome measure. This shows that the evidence is not always uniform, and that effects may vary by study design and outcome measure [N2-F1][N4-F3].

## 9) Whether effects vary by learner background or content depth

The evidence provided is limited on learner background, but it does suggest that effects vary by intervention type. The digital learning designs review notes that the findings must be confirmed in larger controlled trials and that effects vary by intervention type [N2-F1]. The spaced digital education review also did not find strong evidence of differences by learner background, and it reported moderate certainty for knowledge outcomes and low certainty for surgical skills [N4-F3]. The most relevant theoretical outcome in the physiotherapy evidence is that flipped classrooms had a significant effect on knowledge acquisition, while interactive websites/apps and students’ self-produced videos showed significant effects on practical skills [N2-F1].

The strongest theoretical evidence is still concentrated in flipped classrooms and spaced digital education rather than in the more specialized immersive or simulation-based tools cited in the search results [N2-F1][N4-F3].

## 10) How digital tools support or interfere with theoretical knowledge acquisition

Digital tools can support theoretical knowledge acquisition when they incorporate active retrieval and spaced learning. Spaced digital education is explicitly designed to improve long-term retention and recall, and the meta-analysis found that spaced online education was superior to massed online education for postintervention knowledge [N4-F3]. This implies that digital tools should be matched to the learning goal: passive delivery for exposure, but active retrieval and spaced review for retention [N4-F3][N2-F1].

## 11) Practical implication for blended physiotherapy education

For blended physiotherapy education, the most defensible recommendation is to use flipped classrooms and spaced digital education as the core theoretical-learning formats, supported by blended learning structures that combine digital and face-to-face components [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. Video lectures and online modules are useful for content delivery but should be used in ways that promote active learning and spaced review [N2-F1][N5-F4]. Interactive and simulation-based tools are best used for practical skills rather than as the primary vehicle for theoretical knowledge acquisition [N2-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. Blended learning is most effective when curriculum design is coherent, instructor support is strong, and implementation is supported by adequate infrastructure and training [N2-F1][N5-F4].

## 12) Final comparative ranking

Based on the evidence provided, here is a rough comparative ranking for theoretical knowledge acquisition in blended physiotherapy education:

1. **Flipped classrooms** – strongest direct evidence for knowledge acquisition [N2-F1].
2. **Spaced digital education** – especially effective for long-term retention and recall [N4-F3].
3. **Blended learning** – overall most effective digital learning design, especially when flipped classroom principles are embedded [N2-F1][N2-F2].
4. **Video lectures and online modules** – widely used but less clearly superior for theory on their own [N2-F1][N5-F4].
5. **Interactive websites/apps and self-produced videos** – stronger evidence for practical skills than for theoretical knowledge [N2-F1].
6. **Simulations and virtual reality** – promising for practical training, less clearly established for theory [N1-R3][N1-R4].
7. **Distance learning** – no significant difference compared to traditional teaching overall [N2-F1].

## 13) Bottom line

The evidence supports a clear but nuanced conclusion: blended learning and flipped classrooms are the most effective digital learning designs for theoretical knowledge acquisition in physiotherapy education, while spaced learning is especially useful for retention and recall [N2-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3]. Video lectures and online modules are common but less clearly superior on their own; interactive and simulation-based tools are better suited to practical skills [N2-F1][N1-R3][N1-R4]. Implementation quality, curriculum design, and instructor support are critical, and the best outcomes occur when digital tools are used to support active learning and spaced retrieval rather than passive exposure [N2-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].
